newsitem.title: UK: UK GDP data mask unsustainable boom-analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK GDP data mask unsustainable boom-analysts.

text.p: Official growth figures are understating the extent of the current boom in the UK economy and a bust is inevitable unless either monetary or fiscal policy is tightened, analysts warn.

The gross domestic product (GDP) series says the British economy is growing by around 2.5 percent per year -- not far from the 2.0 to 2.5 percent long-term trend rate -- but some inflation hawks believe GDP growth now is closer to a hefty 4.0 percent.

So while Conservative Prime Minister John Major boasts that the economy is growing at a sustainable rate with no sign of inflation, some pundits are drawing comparisons between current economic conditions and those that preceded the late 1980s boom under then Chancellor of the Exchequer Nigel Lawson.
"Even taking into account the figures as they are now, monetary policy has been too loose for too long," said Morgan Stanley UK economist Kevin Gardiner.
"It's another uncanny similarity between where we are now and where we were in the late 1980s," he said.
The Lawson boom, which led to the longest recession since the second world war, did not look like a boom at the time because official data initially showed Britain only experiencing average growth.

Initial estimates showed GDP growing at 3.3 percent in 1985 later revised to 4.0 percent; 2.6 percent in 1986 revised to 4.0 percent; 4.4 percent in 1987 revised to 4.6 percent and 3.8 percent in 1988, revised to 4.9 percent.

"If the data had shown such strength at the time, then the authorities would undoubtedly have tightened policy more quickly and they certainly wouldn't have eased after the 1987 stock market crash," said Lehman Brothers economist Michael Dicks.
By the time the true state of the economy became clear, it was too late to stop the economy overheating, given that changes in monetary policy can take around 18 months to bite into demand.
Analysts warn similar mistakes may be being made at the moment while problems remain on how to assess expenditure with particular reference to the service sector.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has rejected Bank of England requests for a rise in Britain's 6.0 percent interest rate on the grounds that current growth rates are sustainable and that the rise in sterling will keep inflation in check.
Analysts expect interest rates to remain on hold until after the May 1 election but many argue a rise is inevitable at the monetary meeting scheduled for May 10.
The Labour Party is expected to sweep to power after 18 years in opposition and is likely to woo financial markets with an inflation quelling rate rise of around 50 basis points.
But 50 basis points may not be enough. Lehman Brothers UK economist Michael Dicks sees a rate rise of 25 basis points every three months until rates hit 7.5 percent in the first quarter of next year.

Dicks argues that evidence from surveys such as those from the Confederation of British Industry suggests the British economy has now been growing at close to a 4.0 percent annual rate for several quarters.
He says the main concern is that the output gap -- the difference between actual and potential output -- may actually have closed. "This has scary implications for inflation."
The panel of independent Treasury advisers estimated last year that the gap was around 1.5 percent, Dicks said.

Kate Barker, member of the Treasury panel and Chief economic adviser to the Confederation of British Industry, said that she believed there were indeed problems with the official GDP data and that they were probably underestimating the level of growth.

But she was confident the economy was not on the verge of overheating and said the authorities could afford to wait and see how things developed before deciding to put up interest rates. "There is scope to grow above trend for a year without causing problems for inflation," she said.
"We're not finding general skill shortages... distribution is not quite back to 1987 levels. We still have an output gap."

The Office of National Statistics which is responsible for GDP data has made a number of improvements in the way it calculates GDP but it does acknowledge the series has a tendency to underestimate periods of strong growth.
At the moment red lights are flashing in the form of discrepancies between the output, income and expenditures measures of GDP.

The measures should be roughly the same but whilst income and ouput growth were pegged at annual rises of 2.7 and 2.6 percent respectively, the spending based measure was languishing at just 1.7 percent. This suggests either an overestimation of output or an underestimate of expenditure.
Recent history suggests the GDP series has had a tendency to underestimate expenditure because of problems in assessing Britain's energetic and increasingly sophisticated service sector.
